package.title: Compute — HPC統合とmixed-criticalityの現実
package.editorial_angle: ECU削減という物量の話から離れ、mixed criticality、ASIL decomposition、virtualization、resource governance、hardware isolationがHPC統合の上限を決めることを示す。
boundaries: The review does not apply snowballing and excludes some inaccessible/non-English material, including Chinese-language papers and SAE reports; the authors acknowledge publication-bias risk.

The authors note that limited public industry data hinders validation of recent automotive software-architecture advances and that gray literature/expert interviews could improve current-practice coverage.
Best practices transferred from avionics/cloud and the review's applicability outside automotive require further investigation.
The paper shows different start-up behavior on AMD64 and ARM64, so the percentages are not portable across hardware/runtime configurations without retesting.
The authors explicitly find that the best microservice/container count is neither necessarily the maximum nor minimum and must be determined experimentally.
The study is a performance evaluation, not evidence that virtualization/containerization automatically satisfies automotive safety isolation, certification, or deterministic timing requirements.

For simplicity, the model assumes coexistence/freedom-from-interference criteria are satisfied when mixed-criticality tasks share hardware; the optimization does not itself establish the complete safety argument for that coexistence.
Scalability experiments use a fixed four-ECU architecture with randomly generated task graphs and randomized WCET/WCRT/cost values, limiting direct transfer to a production E/E program.
Reported objective values and solver timings are case-study/problem-instance results rather than universal design-space optimization performance.
The paper explicitly focuses on initiator-side mechanisms and defers resource-side developments.
The open-source QEMU/CPU/Bao proof-of-concept is presented as a roadmap rather than completed validation in this paper.
The demonstration is a simulated SDV environment; the authors explicitly identify a more comprehensive demonstration with realistic automotive hardware and software as future work.

The authors note that online integration on the vehicle may be restricted to relatively small problems because vehicle compute resources are limited; larger-scale analysis is better suited to design time.
The PoC predefines VMs because the selected ACRN setup has limited runtime configuration flexibility.

artifact.canonical_name: Towards Mixed-Criticality Software Architectures for Centralized HPC Platforms in Software-Defined Vehicles: A Systematic Literature Review

sources.title: Towards Mixed-Criticality Software Architectures for Centralized HPC Platforms in Software-Defined Vehicles: A Systematic Literature Review
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors conduct a systematic literature review using a documented protocol and qualitative extraction to identify constraints, enabling technologies, techniques and architectural practices for mixed-criticality software on centralized automotive HPC platforms.

The paper frames current E/E evolution as centralized/zonal: functional logic consolidates onto powerful HPCs while zonal gateways aggregate distributed smart I/O, separating compute placement from physical I/O placement.

The review emphasizes hardware resource partitioning, virtualization/isolation, redundancy, scheduling and platform co-design as recurring mechanisms for integrating mixed-criticality workloads on HPC/SoC architectures.

sources.title: Virtualization & Microservice Architecture for Software-Defined Vehicles: An Evaluation and Exploration
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The study evaluates KVM and several container technologies across embedded, AMD64 and ARM64 hardware using CPU, memory, network and disk benchmarks, then tests Autoware and k3s-based microservice decompositions.
The authors report roughly 0-5% CPU/memory/network performance decline versus bare metal in their generic tests, larger disk penalties, and platform-dependent effects for automotive workloads.
The authors find that Autoware start-up can improve under selected microservice decompositions, but the optimal container count is workload/platform specific rather than simply maximized.

artifact.canonical_name: ASIL-Decomposition Based Resource Allocation Optimization for Automotive E/E Architectures

sources.title: ASIL-Decomposition Based Resource Allocation Optimization for Automotive E/E Architectures
sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors formulate automotive software-to-hardware mapping, scheduling and ASIL decomposition as a single mixed-integer linear optimization problem targeting development cost and critical-chain execution time while applying safety/reliability constraints.

The exemplary case study exposes a cost/latency trade-off: prioritizing development cost yields lower cost with longer maximum application execution time, while prioritizing latency increases cost and reduces that execution time.
The authors compare Gurobi and CPLEX and report that solving time grows as task count increases; ASIL decomposition cases can materially increase optimization time.
claims.context: Generated/evaluated problem instances, not production design-cycle measurements.

artifact.organization: OSYX Technologies / Universidade do Minho / Infineon AG

sources.title: RISC-V Needs Secure 'Wheels': the MCU Initiator-Side Perspective
sources.role: Author arXiv paper/preprint used to verify the architecture, evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors tie centralized/domain/zone E/E evolution to increasing integration density, where formerly separate ECUs become virtualized logical partitions on fewer physical MCUs and require freedom-from-interference.
The paper argues that then-current RISC-V WorldGuard/SPMP proposals are insufficient for foreseen automotive virtualized-MCU isolation and proposes hypervisor-aware initiator-side extensions.
claims.context: Author technical critique/proposal, not a ratified ISA fact.

claims.text: The proposed Slwgd/related register extensions expand the WorldGuard identifier model toward 64/128 IDs and add virtualized privilege-level delegation support.

metrics.context: Proposed extension capacity; not a ratified WorldGuard requirement.

metrics.context: Author-estimated upper-threshold example based on harts, privilege levels and non-CPU initiators.

limitations.text: The paper explicitly focuses on initiator-side mechanisms and defers resource-side developments.
The open-source QEMU/CPU/Bao proof-of-concept is presented as a roadmap rather than completed validation in this paper.

targets.target: Verify the architecture, evaluation setup, material claims and limitations reported for RISC-V Needs Secure 'Wheels': the MCU Initiator-Side Perspective; preserve paper results as AUTHOR_CLAIM unless independently established.
targets.finding: The full primary text verifies the automotive virtualization/isolation motivation, WorldGuard/SPMP gaps, proposed hypervisor/ID extensions, 128-ID target and explicit PoC/resource-side future-work boundary.

editorial.why_now_note: As ECU consolidation increases mixed-criticality co-location, hardware isolation capability becomes an E/E architectural constraint rather than a local MCU implementation detail.
editorial.rationale: Strong compute-isolation evidence for consolidating formerly separate ECUs into virtualized MCU partitions, while clearly remaining a proposal/roadmap rather than completed proof-of-concept.

sources.role: Author paper/preprint used to verify the reported architecture, method/evaluation scope, material claims, and limitations available in the primary text.

claims.text: The authors move platform configuration and software integration toward runtime using an integration manager that combines model-based design-space exploration, code generation, hypervisor partitions, containers, orchestration, and a REST interface.
claims.context: Proposed architecture and implemented proof of concept.

claims.text: The proof-of-concept architecture uses ACRN VMs to separate execution environments and containers within user VMs for application deployment, with predefined constraints used to verify and optimize integration plans.
claims.context: Implemented PoC architecture; this is not evidence of a certified freedom-from-interference argument.

claims.text: The PoC uses an Intel Whiskey Lake board with a Service VM and two User VMs and demonstrates a two-step online integration scenario that adds applications while preserving an existing deployment.
